q: The state says an EMT may give a drug. The medical director says no. Who is final?

opts.t: The medical director; both state scope and their protocols must allow it
opts.why: The director can say no even if the state says yes.

opts.t: The state list alone
opts.why: Protocols can still shut it down.

opts.t: The patient, if they ask for it
opts.why: Asking is not a protocol.

opts.t: Any nurse on scene
opts.why: The medical director owns the yes or no.

q: What is pharmacodynamics?

opts.t: What the drug does to the body: receptors to a treatment effect
opts.why: Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body.

opts.t: The life cycle: onset, peak, duration, elimination
opts.why: That is pharmacokinetics.

opts.t: The five rights only
opts.why: The five rights are a safety check, not this word.

opts.t: The brand name on the box
opts.why: A name is not pharmacodynamics.

q: Epinephrine as an agonist. Which pairing?

opts.t: Alpha squeezes vessels; beta-1 raises heart rate and squeeze; beta-2 opens airways
opts.why: Alpha = vasoconstriction. Beta-1 = 1 heart. Beta-2 = 2 lungs.

opts.t: Alpha opens airways; beta-1 squeezes vessels; beta-2 slows the heart
opts.why: Those jobs are mixed up.

opts.t: All three only block narcotic receptors
opts.why: That block is naloxone.

opts.t: Alpha dissolves clots; beta-1 and beta-2 do nothing
opts.why: Aspirin is the platelet drug, and it does not dissolve clots.

q: Naloxone job?

opts.t: Narcotic receptor antagonist; reverses opioid overdose
opts.why: Same-shape bind, blocks instead of firing.

opts.t: Alpha agonist that raises blood pressure only
opts.why: That squeeze is epinephrine's alpha job.

opts.t: Beta-2 agonist for simple asthma
opts.why: That is albuterol.

opts.t: Platelet blocker for chest pain
opts.why: That is aspirin.

q: Pharmacokinetics life cycle, and why onset matters?

opts.t: Onset, peak, duration, elimination; onset says when to reassess
opts.why: Onset is admin to starts-working. That clock drives the recheck.

opts.t: Indication, contraindication, side effect, brand; onset is ignored
opts.why: Those are other words. Onset is when to reassess.

opts.t: Patient, medication, dose, route; onset is the brand name
opts.why: Those are rights, not the life cycle.

opts.t: IV, IO, IM, IN; onset is always 20 to 30 minutes
opts.why: IV is immediate. 20-30 minutes is a swallowed pill.

q: Route and timing pair?

opts.t: IV is immediate; a swallowed pill is about 20 to 30 minutes
opts.why: Route changes the clock.

opts.t: A swallowed pill is immediate; IV is 20 to 30 minutes
opts.why: Those are swapped.

opts.t: Both take 6 hours
opts.why: About 6 hours is how long carbon monoxide can stay bound, not these routes.

opts.t: Both take 10 seconds
opts.why: 10 seconds is a suction cap.

q: Indication versus contraindication?

opts.t: Indication is a reason to give it; contraindication is a reason not to
opts.why: For EMT meds, treat contraindications as absolute unless a doctor overrides.

opts.t: Indication is a reason not to; contraindication is a reason to give it
opts.why: Those are swapped.

opts.t: Both mean side effects after the drug is in
opts.why: Side effects are unintended results, not the yes/no gate.

opts.t: Both mean the brand name
opts.why: A name is not a reason.

q: What naming does the National Registry want?

opts.t: Generic names, usually lowercase: naloxone, epinephrine
opts.why: Brand is owned and capitalized: Narcan, EpiPen.

opts.t: Brand names only: Narcan, EpiPen
opts.why: The registry wants generic.

opts.t: Only the store brand on the shelf
opts.why: Generic is the test name.

opts.t: Either name, as long as the dose is skipped
opts.why: Dose still matters, and the name they want is generic.

q: Nitroglycerin route, and why it is fast?

opts.t: Under the tongue; that tissue is very vascular
opts.why: Sublingual. Do not swallow it right away.

opts.t: Swallowed pill; 20 to 30 minutes
opts.why: Swallowing it wastes the fast route.

opts.t: Intranasal, like naloxone
opts.why: Nitro is under the tongue.

opts.t: Intramuscular lateral thigh
opts.why: That is the EpiPen route.

q: What are the original five rights?

opts.t: Right patient, medication, dose, route, and time
opts.why: Time includes expiration, hold time, and how often a repeat is allowed.

opts.t: Right brand, color, box, truck, and city
opts.why: Those are not the five rights.

opts.t: Right onset, peak, duration, elimination, and brand
opts.why: That mix is pharmacokinetics plus a name.

opts.t: Right indication only
opts.why: Indication is why. The five rights are the check.

q: What must be documented after a med is given?

opts.t: Name, dose, route, time, and how they responded
opts.why: Write what went in and what it did.

opts.t: Brand color only
opts.why: Color is not the record.

opts.t: Only the generic name, no dose
opts.why: Dose, route, time, and response stay.

opts.t: Nothing if they got better
opts.why: Still document.

q: Sugar 68, follows commands, can swallow. Oral glucose?

opts.t: Yes: under 80, awake, airway protected; one tube
opts.why: Tubes often 15 g (range 15-25 g). Say one tube. Recheck sugar. Test answer is oral glucose, not juice.

opts.t: No: under 80 is not low enough
opts.why: Under 80 is the hypoglycemia cut.

opts.t: No: they are awake, so wait for IV dextrose
opts.why: Awake and swallowing is when the gel is allowed.

opts.t: Yes, but only if they are unresponsive
opts.why: Unresponsive is the hold.

q: Low sugar, only responds to pain, gurgling. Why hold oral glucose?

opts.t: Cannot protect the airway; gel in the lungs is aspiration
opts.why: Unconscious or cannot swallow = no oral glucose. Paramedics and the ED use IV dextrose.

opts.t: Sugar 68 is too high for any sugar
opts.why: The hold is the airway, not a 68.

opts.t: Glucose only comes as a swallowed aspirin tablet
opts.why: Glucose is a gel. Aspirin is the chest-pain tablet.

opts.t: Hold it only if systolic pressure is over 100
opts.why: That pressure rule is nitro, not glucose.

q: Aspirin on suspected heart-attack chest. What does it do, and what does it not do?

opts.t: Makes platelets slippery so a clot does not grow; it does not dissolve clots
opts.why: Stops platelets from clumping. Not a clot-buster.

opts.t: Dissolves the clot on contact
opts.why: It does not dissolve clots.

opts.t: Opens airways as a beta-2 agonist
opts.why: That is albuterol or epi's beta-2 job.

opts.t: Blocks narcotic receptors
opts.why: That is naloxone.

q: Aspirin test dose and how it is given?

opts.t: 160 to 325 mg by mouth, chewed
opts.why: Tablets are 81 mg. Adult 162-324 mg from 2-4 tablets. Test: 160-325 chewed, then swallowed.

opts.t: 0.4 mg under the tongue
opts.why: That is nitro.

opts.t: 0.3 mg in the lateral thigh
opts.why: That is adult epinephrine.

opts.t: One tube of gel in the cheek
opts.why: That is oral glucose.

q: Nitroglycerin dose, route, and repeat rule?

opts.t: 0.4 mg under the tongue, up to 3 doses, 5 minutes apart
opts.why: Check blood pressure before every dose. Stop if systolic is under 100 or pain is gone.

opts.t: 160 to 325 mg chewed, one dose only
opts.why: That is aspirin.

opts.t: 0.3 mg in the thigh every 5 minutes, no max
opts.why: 0.3 mg IM is adult epi, and nitro has a max of 3.

opts.t: One tube of gel every 20 to 30 minutes
opts.why: That mix is glucose plus a pill clock.

q: Which cluster kills nitro?

opts.t: Systolic pressure under 100, a -fil sex drug in 24 hours, or a head injury
opts.why: Need triple-digit systolic. Combined vasodilators crash pressure. Head injury is a no.

opts.t: Pulse ox 96 percent and no chest pain
opts.why: No pain is a reason to stop or not start, but the named kill cluster is pressure, -fil, head.

opts.t: Sugar under 80 and they can swallow
opts.why: That picture is oral glucose, not a nitro kill.

opts.t: Hives plus wheeze
opts.why: That is anaphylaxis, an epi picture.

q: Nitro side effects and handling?

opts.t: Headache is common; low blood pressure is the dangerous one; wear gloves
opts.why: Nitro absorbs through skin. Also burn under the tongue and nausea.

opts.t: No side effects; bare hands are required
opts.why: Gloves on. Pressure drop is the danger.

opts.t: Only a dry nose; no pressure check
opts.why: Check pressure before every dose.

opts.t: Only pinpoint pupils
opts.why: Pinpoints are an opioid clue, not a nitro effect.

q: One nitro is already in. When may the next one be given?

opts.t: Systolic still at least 100, pain still there, wait 5 minutes, max 3 total
opts.why: Give one, then move. Do not sit on scene for all three.

opts.t: Any pressure, even 80, if they still hurt
opts.why: Stop if systolic is under 100.

opts.t: Right away, no wait, no max
opts.why: Wait 5 minutes. Max 3.

opts.t: Only after 20 to 30 minutes, like a swallowed pill
opts.why: The repeat clock is 5 minutes, not 20-30.

q: Hives plus wheezing. Anaphylaxis or not?

opts.t: Anaphylaxis: two systems, skin plus breathing
opts.why: Allergic reaction in two or more systems. Hives only is not.

opts.t: Not anaphylaxis, because hives only never counts with wheeze
opts.why: Hives plus wheeze is two systems.

opts.t: Not anaphylaxis, because that word needs a heart-attack story
opts.why: Heart attack is an aspirin / nitro story.

opts.t: Anaphylaxis only if they also took a -fil drug
opts.why: A -fil drug is a nitro hold, not an anaphylaxis rule.

q: Hives only, no breathing or shock trouble. Epi?

opts.t: No. That is not anaphylaxis
opts.why: Hives only is not two systems. Do not hunt epi orders.

opts.t: Yes. Any rash gets 0.3 mg
opts.why: Epi is for anaphylaxis, not a mild allergy.

opts.t: Yes, because simple asthma also gets epi
opts.why: Simple asthma gets albuterol, not epi.

opts.t: Yes, if systolic pressure is under 100
opts.why: Low pressure can be shock, but hives only is still not the two-system call.

q: Adult versus junior epinephrine auto-injector?

opts.t: Adult 0.3 mg IM lateral thigh; junior 0.15 mg IM
opts.why: Lateral thigh. Can go through one layer of clothes.

opts.t: Adult 0.15 mg under the tongue; junior 0.3 mg chewed
opts.why: Those numbers and routes are mixed with nitro and aspirin.

opts.t: Adult 0.4 mg IM; junior one tube of gel
opts.why: 0.4 mg is nitro. Gel is glucose.

opts.t: Both are 160 to 325 mg chewed
opts.why: That is aspirin.

q: How is an adult EpiPen fired?

opts.t: Safety off, blue to the sky, orange to the lateral thigh, click, hold about 3 seconds
opts.why: One clothing layer is okay.

opts.t: Orange to the sky, blue to the neck, no hold
opts.why: Orange to the thigh. Hold about 3 seconds.

opts.t: Spray it under the tongue like nitro
opts.why: Epi is intramuscular.

opts.t: Chew 81 mg, then hold 3 seconds
opts.why: 81 mg is an aspirin tablet.

q: Very high blood pressure on an 'allergy' patient. Why hold epi?

opts.t: Epi raises pressure; high plus higher can burst pipes
opts.why: Stroke / bleed risk. True anaphylaxis is usually low, not high.

opts.t: Epi always drops pressure, so high pressure is required first
opts.why: Epi raises pressure.

opts.t: High pressure is a nitro start, so give nitro instead
opts.why: Nitro is a chest-pain drug with a low-pressure hold.

opts.t: High pressure means they need oral glucose
opts.why: Glucose is a sugar-and-airway drug.

q: Severe hypothermia. Why is epi extra dangerous?

opts.t: That heart is extra sensitive; even rough movement can arrest, and epi can push them into arrest
opts.why: Hold or be very careful in hypothermia.

opts.t: Hypothermia always needs more epi, no caution
opts.why: The caution is the sensitive heart.

opts.t: Hypothermia is treated with aspirin only
opts.why: Aspirin is the platelet chest-pain drug.

opts.t: Hypothermia is a reason to skip all airway work
opts.why: Airway still matters. This question is the epi caution.

q: Known heart attack. Why be careful with epi?

opts.t: Epi makes the heart work harder and can worsen the damage
opts.why: MI / known heart attack is a named caution.

opts.t: Epi dissolves the clot, so it replaces aspirin
opts.why: Epi does not dissolve clots, and aspirin does not either.

opts.t: Epi is required for every chest pain
opts.why: Chest pain is aspirin / nitro, not a default epi.

opts.t: Epi is the same as a 0.4 mg nitro spray
opts.why: Different drug, different job.

q: Straightforward asthma attack. Epi or not?

opts.t: Do not use epi; use albuterol
opts.why: Epi is for anaphylaxis, not simple asthma.

opts.t: Fire epi first, skip albuterol
opts.why: Simple asthma is an albuterol job.

opts.t: Give nitro because airways are vessels
opts.why: Nitro is a chest-pain vasodilator.

opts.t: Give oral glucose to open the bronchi
opts.why: Glucose is sugar, not a bronchodilator.

q: Naloxone reverses which family?

opts.t: Opioids only: heroin, fentanyl, morphine, oxycodone, Vicodin
opts.why: It will not reverse alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other non-opioid sedatives.

opts.t: Alcohol, Valium, and Xanax
opts.why: Those are not opioids.

opts.t: Any allergy, including hives only
opts.why: Allergy / anaphylaxis is an epi story.

opts.t: Any chest pain
opts.why: Chest pain is aspirin / nitro.

q: Intranasal naloxone. Why can it still work if they are not breathing?

opts.t: It absorbs through nasal mucosa into blood; it is not a lung drug
opts.why: IN is most common. It does not need them to inhale it.

opts.t: They must inhale it into the alveoli first
opts.why: It is not a lung inhale drug.

opts.t: It only works after a 20 to 30 minute pill clock
opts.why: IN is rapid.

opts.t: It only works if they can swallow gel
opts.why: Swallowing is a glucose rule, not naloxone.

q: EMT naloxone dose to memorize?

opts.t: None; it varies by route and packaging. Follow the device and protocol
opts.why: No single standard EMT dose was given to lock.

opts.t: 0.4 mg under the tongue, max 3
opts.why: That is nitro.

opts.t: 0.3 mg IM for every adult, no protocol
opts.why: 0.3 mg IM is adult epi.

opts.t: 160 to 325 mg chewed
opts.why: That is aspirin.

q: Opioid-overdose look?

opts.t: Low blood pressure, low heart rate, slow or no breaths, down mental status; pinpoint pupils classic but not required
opts.why: A trial that works points to opioid. No change means other cause or a heavy load.

opts.t: High pressure, fast deep Kussmaul, hives only
opts.why: That mix is not the opioid picture.

opts.t: Chest pain that improves after one nitro, no breathing trouble
opts.why: That is a cardiac-pain story.

opts.t: Sugar 68, talking, no breathing trouble
opts.why: That is a glucose picture.

q: After naloxone, what should improve first, and what side effects?

opts.t: Breathing rate and depth, then mental status; they can wake nauseated, vomiting, or combative
opts.why: Scene safety as they come up. Prefer IN around IV drug users to skip needles.

opts.t: Chest pain first; no side effects
opts.why: Naloxone is not a chest-pain drug.

opts.t: Sugar first; they always stay asleep
opts.why: The goal is air, then mind. They can wake fighting.

opts.t: Platelets first; they always seize
opts.why: Platelets are an aspirin story.

q: Albuterol class and job?

opts.t: Beta-2 agonist: bronchodilation for asthma / bronchospasm
opts.why: Less whole-body punch than epi, and the right tool for asthma.

opts.t: Narcotic antagonist
opts.why: That is naloxone.

opts.t: Platelet blocker
opts.why: That is aspirin.

opts.t: Vasodilator under the tongue
opts.why: That is nitro.

q: Metered-dose inhaler assist. What is the timing point?

opts.t: Spray as they inhale so it reaches lung
opts.why: Spray off-time coats the mouth and does nothing. Kids may need a spacer.

opts.t: Spray while they hold a full exhale only
opts.why: It has to ride an inhale.

opts.t: Spray under the tongue like nitro
opts.why: MDI is inhaled.

opts.t: Spray into the lateral thigh
opts.why: Thigh is the EpiPen.

q: Small-volume nebulizer setup?

opts.t: 6 liters per minute oxygen through liquid albuterol; continuous mist
opts.why: They breathe again and again. Deeper dose than one MDI puff.

opts.t: 1 liter per minute through nitro spray
opts.why: Nitro is not a neb drug, and 1 L is a cannula play.

opts.t: 10 to 15 liters through an empty cup, no drug
opts.why: The cup holds liquid albuterol. 10-15 is a mask/bag flow.

opts.t: No oxygen; just shake a gel tube into the cup
opts.why: Gel is glucose. The neb needs oxygen flow and albuterol.

q: EMT medication list?

opts.t: Aspirin, nitroglycerin, oral glucose, epinephrine, naloxone, albuterol
opts.why: Limited to that list. Tylenol or Benadryl are not yours unless written into protocol.

opts.t: Tylenol, Benadryl, fentanyl, and any nurse med
opts.why: OTC is not default EMT. Fentanyl is not on this EMT list.

opts.t: Only aspirin and nothing else
opts.why: Six were named.

opts.t: Only paramedic intubation drugs
opts.why: Intubation is a medic skill contrast, not the EMT list.

q: Wrong med is already in. First four moves?

opts.t: Take care of the patient, call medical control honest, document facts, then agency follow-up
opts.why: Cannot un-give a drug. Patient first. Factual, objective, honest.

opts.t: Hide it, then wait for the next shift
opts.why: Call medical control now.

opts.t: Document a different drug, then leave the scene
opts.why: Document what actually happened.

opts.t: Give a second outside-scope drug to cancel the first
opts.why: Do not stack a scope break.

q: Big legal red line?

opts.t: Giving a drug outside EMT scope, or something state and protocol forbid
opts.why: Discipline, state report, card at risk, legal action if they are hurt.

opts.t: Documenting name, dose, route, time, and response
opts.why: That record is required, not a red line.

opts.t: Calling medical control after a real error
opts.why: That call is the right move.

opts.t: Holding oral glucose when they cannot swallow
opts.why: That hold is correct.

q: Enteral versus parenteral?

opts.t: Enteral goes through the gut; parenteral is anything not through the gut
opts.why: PO swallow is slow. SL nitro is still enteral but fast. IV, IO, IM, IN, inhaled are parenteral.

opts.t: Enteral is IV only; parenteral is a swallowed pill only
opts.why: Those are swapped ideas.

opts.t: Both mean brand names
opts.why: These words are routes, not names.

opts.t: Both mean the five rights
opts.why: Rights are a safety check.
